title: Linear and generalized linear models (OLS + GLM families)
procedure: Ordinary least squares and the generalized linear model under one interface. OLS estimates the coefficient vector beta minimizing the residual sum of squares for a Gaussian-error linear model, reporting standard errors, t-statistics, p-values, R-squared and the residual standard error. The GLM extends this to non-Gaussian responses (binomial, Poisson, Gamma, negative binomial) via a link function, estimating beta by maximum likelihood and reporting standard errors, Wald z/t-statistics, p-values, deviance and AIC. pystatistics deliberately unifies lm and glm — which R splits across lm() and glm() — into a single fit(design, family=...) entry point.
algorithms: OLS, CPU (reference path): column-pivoted QR decomposition of the design matrix (the same factorization R's lm() uses), so coefficients, rank detection and the residual statistics match R to floating-point round-off. fp64, deterministic.

OLS, GPU: Cholesky factorization of the normal equations (X'X) beta = X'y, fp32 by default on consumer GPUs. Faster than QR for well-conditioned designs but squares the condition number; the backend computes the design's condition number and refuses the Cholesky path (unless force=True) when it exceeds 1e6, falling back to a least-squares solve.

GLM (all families): Iteratively Reweighted Least Squares (IRLS / Fisher scoring) to the maximum-likelihood coefficients, with R's glm.control defaults (tol 1e-8, max 25 iterations). Standard errors come from the inverse Fisher information at the solution.
Negative binomial: the dispersion parameter theta is estimated by profiling — alternating an IRLS fit of beta at fixed theta with a maximum-likelihood update of theta — mirroring MASS::glm.nb.
Backends: cpu (fp64, the R-reference path) and gpu (MPS on Apple Silicon, CUDA on NVIDIA; fp32 by default, fp64 on CUDA where supported).

reference.name: R stats::lm / stats::glm / MASS::glm.nb
reference.what: R's lm() (OLS via pivoted QR) and glm() (GLM via IRLS) are the established reference implementations; the negative-binomial reference is MASS::glm.nb. Because pystatistics merges lm and glm into one module, the head-to-head pulls from BOTH R functions: lm() for the OLS claim and glm()/glm.nb() for the GLM-family claims. Agreement in coefficients, standard errors, test statistics, p-values, and the model-level fit summary (R-squared for OLS, deviance for GLM) is the correctness claim.

tolerances.ols_vs_r: CPU OLS agrees with R lm() to fp64 round-off (coefficients and standard errors to ~1e-12 relative or better) because both use pivoted QR on the same design.
tolerances.glm_vs_r: CPU GLM coefficients agree with R glm() to IRLS-convergence round-off (~1e-10 relative for binomial/Poisson). Standard errors and Wald statistics follow the coefficients.
tolerances.gamma_link: The Gamma claim is specifically for the LOG link (the textbook positive-continuous target). pystatistics' family='gamma' string defaults to the canonical INVERSE link; the validation pins GammaFamily(link='log') to match the reference. Gamma standard errors differ from R at the ~1e-2 relative level because pystatistics estimates the dispersion by maximum likelihood while R uses the Pearson/df estimator — a documented, intentional difference, not a defect.
tolerances.negbin: Negative-binomial coefficients agree with MASS::glm.nb to ~1e-4 relative; the small gap is the profiled theta landing at a slightly different value. The NB mean structure is identified only up to theta, so coefficient agreement on real overdispersed counts is the practical claim.
tolerances.gpu_fp32: GPU paths are fp32 by default and agree with the CPU/R reference to ~1e-4 relative on coefficients; for full fp64 precision use the CPU backend (or CUDA fp64 where supported).

limitations: GPU OLS uses Cholesky on the normal equations, which squares the condition number; ill-conditioned designs (condition number > 1e6) are refused unless force=True. Use the CPU QR backend for ill-conditioned problems.
GPU paths are fp32 by default; MPS does not support fp64 at all. Applications needing full double precision must use the CPU backend.
The negative-binomial solution object does not expose the auto-estimated theta, so the NB validation compares coefficients (and SEs) rather than theta directly.

Tiny designs (n in the low hundreds) are dominated by fixed Python dispatch overhead and sit near R's timer resolution; the scaling study, not the small real datasets, carries the rigorous speed claim.

datasets.name: California Housing
datasets.what: ~20,640 California census blocks, 8 numeric predictors. Used for OLS (MedHouseVal ~ all predictors), binomial (high_value, a median split) and Poisson (pop_count = round(Population/100)). Large enough to exercise the QR and IRLS paths on a non-trivial real design.

datasets.name: airquality
datasets.what: datasets::airquality — daily NYC air quality, 111 complete cases. Gamma(log) target Ozone ~ Solar.R + Temp + Wind; ozone is positive, continuous and right-skewed, the textbook Gamma regression target.

datasets.name: quine
datasets.what: MASS::quine — 146 Australian schoolchildren, days absent by ethnicity/sex/age/learner status. THE canonical negative-binomial dataset (McCullagh & Nelder). The R model matrix is handed to Python so both engines fit the identical numeric design.

datasets.name: synthetic scaling grid
datasets.what: Deterministic Gaussian designs over n in {1e3, 1e4, 1e5, 5e5} x p in {8, 32, 128} for OLS and binomial, used only for the device-scaling/performance study (not correctness).
